can.verb type: **modal auxiliary** — never a main verb: it takes a bare infinitive (*can carry*), has no *-s*, no *-ing*, and no participle (✗ *he cans*, ✗ *I have could*, ✗ *to can*), so *be able to* fills the perfect and infinitive slots. A separate, fully regular action verb *can* means "put food in cans."
can.transitivity: **neither transitive nor intransitive** in the ordinary sense — a modal takes a bare-infinitive complement, not an object: *I can carry both bags*. The only nominal object it ever shows is the fixed *he can't help it*.
can.passive: **no** — modals have no passive of their own; voice is carried by the verb they support (*the bags can be carried*), never by *can* itself.

clothe.verb type: **action** — dynamic in every sense, from supplying clothing (*the shelter clothes and feeds them*) to covering a surface (*snow clad the hills*). The participle *clad* now does most of its work as an adjective: *scantily clad*, *ivy-clad*.
clothe.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is obligatory: *clothe the children*, ✗ *the shelter clothed* on its own. The facing sense adds *in*: *they clad the new tower in blue glass*.
clothe.passive: **yes**, and the *be clad in* sense is normally passive — *the reactor core is clad in steel*, *every wall of the lobby had been clad in walnut*.

flee.verb type: **action** — dynamic throughout, including the literary use with abstract subjects: *sleep fled the moment the phone rang*, *all the color had fled her face*.
flee.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a bare object in edited American prose (*fled the city*, *fled the scene*, *fled the country*), intransitive or with *from* when the danger is left unnamed (*families flee whenever a hurricane is forecast*).
flee.passive: **restricted** — grammatical but avoided: ✗ *the scene was fled by the driver* reads badly, and writers keep the active. The intransitive use has no passive at all.

foretell.verb type: **action** with a human subject prophesying (*two economists foretold the collapse*); closer to **stative** with an inanimate subject that merely points to an outcome — *nothing in the data foretells a crash*, ✗ *the data is foretelling a crash*.
foretell.transitivity: **transitive** — object obligatory, either a noun or a *that*-clause: *foretold his own retirement*, *foretold that the deal would fail*. ✗ *He foretold* alone is incomplete.
foretell.passive: **yes** — *the collapse was foretold and nobody listened*; *the ending had been foretold in the opening chapter*.

hear.verb type: **stative** in the core perception sense, which rejects the progressive: ✗ *I am hearing you* — say *I can hear you*. **Action** in the deliberate institutional senses *hear a case*, *hear the testimony*, *hear someone out*.
hear.transitivity: **transitive** — the object may be a noun, a *that*-clause, or a small clause (*nobody heard the alarm go off*). It is intransitive only with a preposition attached: *hear from the landlord*, *hear of that band*, *wouldn't hear of it*.
hear.passive: **yes** — *the alarm was heard three blocks away*, *the committee heard testimony* → *testimony was heard for six hours*, *the senator was heard to say it*. Even the prepositional sense passivizes in the fixed *he has not been heard from since April*.

mishear.verb type: **action** — dynamic and momentary, a single mishap rather than the ongoing state of *hear*: *I misheard the gate number*.
mishear.transitivity: **transitive**, often with an *as*-complement (*she had misheard "fifteen" as "fifty"*). The object drops when it is recoverable — *I must have misheard* is complete.
mishear.passive: **restricted** — natural in the *as* frame (*the name is regularly misheard as Cohen*), but the verb lives in the active perfect *must have misheard*, and ✗ *I was misheard by him* is barely used.

outsell.verb type: **action** — dynamic, reporting a result over a period: *trucks outsell sedans in most of the country*.
outsell.transitivity: **transitive** — object obligatory, and it names the rival or the rival's product, never the goods you moved: *outsold Ford*, *outsold every other pickup*, ✗ *outsold ten thousand trucks*.
outsell.passive: **yes**, though the active carries most of the traffic: *sedans are outsold by trucks nearly everywhere*, *the hardcover was outsold ten to one*.

overhear.verb type: **action** — dynamic but involuntary; deliberate listening is the separate regular verb *eavesdrop*. Commonly takes an *-ing* clause: *overheard two nurses talking*.
overhear.transitivity: **transitive** — object obligatory: *in an open office you overhear everything*, *they had overheard the whole argument*. ✗ *I overheard* alone leaves the sentence hanging.
overhear.passive: **yes**, and the passive is a journalistic staple: *the senator was overheard telling an aide the deal was dead*, *he has been overheard complaining more than once*.

oversell.verb type: **action** — dynamic in both the capacity sense (*airlines oversell popular routes*) and the hype sense (*don't oversell the feature*). The participle *oversold* is also a finance adjective: *the index looks oversold*.
oversell.transitivity: **transitive** — *the venue oversold the show by two hundred seats*, *the company has oversold this product for years*; the object is normally required.
oversell.passive: **yes**, and it is the usual form when the booking lands on you: *our flight had been oversold*, *traders had oversold the sector* → *the sector had been oversold by spring*.

rehear.verb type: **action** — dynamic and narrowly institutional: an appellate court takes a matter back up. Not a word for playing a recording again.
rehear.transitivity: **transitive** — object obligatory and restricted to a case, an appeal, or arguments: *rehear the appeal en banc*, ✗ *rehear the album* (say *listen to it again*).
rehear.passive: **yes** — *the case has been reheard twice*, *the arguments had been reheard and nothing changed*; the passive is as common as the active in opinions.

resell.verb type: **action** — dynamic in all senses, including the figurative *resell the board on a plan they had already approved*.
resell.transitivity: **transitive** — object obligatory: *resell them at four times face value*, *resells refurbished laptops*. The persuasion sense adds an *on*-phrase: *resold the whole team on the deadline*.
resell.passive: **yes** — *the apartment had been resold twice before we ever saw it*; *the same painting has been resold three times*.

retell.verb type: **action** — dynamic; the *-ing* form doubles as a noun, *a modern retelling of the myth*.
retell.transitivity: **transitive**, and unlike *tell* it is not ditransitive: the object must be the story, never the listener — *retold the joke badly*, ✗ *retell them the address* (say *tell them again*).
retell.passive: **yes** — *the story has been retold on stage, on film, and in a graphic novel*.

seethe.verb type: **action** — dynamic, a continuing process, and comfortable in the progressive: *the sidewalk was seething with tourists*. Modern American forms are regular (*seethed*, *have seethed*); ✗ *the crowd sod*.
seethe.transitivity: **intransitive** in every live sense — *he seethes*, *the station seethed with commuters* — and what it churns with follows *with*. Only the dead archaic "boil something" sense was transitive: *Jacob sod pottage*.
seethe.passive: **no** — an intransitive verb has no passive: ✗ *the meeting was seethed through*. The archaic transitive use left behind only the adjective *sodden*.

sell.verb type: **action** — dynamic throughout, including the figurative *sell someone on an idea* and *sell yourself* in an interview.
sell.transitivity: **both** — ditransitive or transitive with *to* (*sold a neighbor the truck* / *sold the truck to a neighbor*), and intransitive with the merchandise as subject, usually with an adverb or a figure (*winter coats sell fast*, *the album sold two million copies*).
sell.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the house has been sold twice since we moved out*, *I am not sold on the new design*. The goods-as-subject use has no matching passive: *winter coats sell fast* is not ✗ *winter coats are sold fast*.

shoe.verb type: **action** — dynamic; the participle *shod* now does most of its work as an adjective (*well-shod*, *steel-shod*) and survives frozen in *ride roughshod over*.
shoe.transitivity: **transitive** — object obligatory: *shoe a horse in half an hour*, *fed and shod everyone who came through the door*. ✗ *The farrier shod* alone is incomplete.
shoe.passive: **yes**, and it is the common form — *every horse in the barn has been shod this season*, *the mare had been shod badly and had gone lame*.

tell.verb type: **action** — dynamic in the reporting, narrating, and instructing senses; closer to **stative** in *can tell* "perceive, work out," which leans on a modal and rejects the progressive: ✗ *I am telling the twins apart*.
tell.transitivity: **ditransitive** at its core, with the listener bare and obligatory — *told me the flight had been canceled*, ✗ *told to me*, ✗ *He told that he was late*. Also plain transitive in the fixed list (*tell the truth*, *tell time*) and intransitive with *on* (*the years have told on that engine*).
tell.passive: **yes** — *we were told to stay in the car*, *I have never been told off like that in my life*. The listener is the natural passive subject: *she was told the news*, while *the news was told to her* is stiff.

undersell.verb type: **action** — dynamic, comparing price (*the chain undersold every local shop*) or the fit between a description and its subject (*the brochure badly undersells the view*).
undersell.transitivity: **transitive** — object obligatory, naming the rival or the thing described, not the price: *undersell them on lumber*, *undersells the view*, reflexive in *don't undersell yourself*.
undersell.passive: **yes** — *every local shop was undersold by the chain*. The "understate" sense passivizes less comfortably and is usually left in the active: *reviewers have undersold how strange the film is*.
